4 Pitch control
This function allows fine adjustment of pifth (up to +8%).
1. Press the pitch control switch to ‘‘on”.
The pitch control indicator illuminates.
2. Slide the pitch control knob upward or downward
to the desired setting.
@When not using this function, press the pitch control switch
again to release it (off).
Note:
In the center position (>) a “click” can be perceived.
This position is the 0% standard pitch.
The +5.9% position is a half tone sharp (+ ).
The —5.6% position is a half tone flat ( b).
When the pitch has been changed, the elapsed or remaining
playing time readings will differ from the actual times by the
amount of pitch adjustment.
5 Skip play
(Skip play can be performed when the player is
in the play or pause mode.)
This function allows quick access to the beginning of a track.
Note: Index skip play is not possible.
Forward skip
eThe pickup skips the same number of tracks as the number of
times the button is pressed.
During automatic play, the pickup skips to the beginning of the
next track each time the button is pressed.
eDuring program play or program repeat play, the pickup skips
to the beginning of the next programmed track each time the
button is pressed.
While watching the track number display, press the forward
skip button until the desired track has been located.

About rocking search
When two or more CD players are used at a time, as often
happens in a studio for example, fade-in and fade-out of
the units have to be timed exactly. The rocking search
function is useful for this because it permits movement of
the pickup across one pit-track (at inner diameter in about
0.13 second) each time either button is pressed momen-
tarily.

9 Auto cue function
(automatic standby)
Auto cue function
At the beginning of each track on most discs, a silent interval of
about one second is recorded. Therefore, when play is started
from Q min. 00 sec, music is not heard immediately.
When the auto cue function is activated, the unit automatically
detects the beginning of the music on each track and then
switches to standby mode.
When play is started from this point (by pressing the play button)
music is heard immediately.

1. TRAVERSE MECHANISM and OPTICAL PICKUP
1-1 Traverse Mechanism
Fig. 1-1 shows the traverse mechanism.
The traverse mechanism conveys power from the motor to the wormgear, gear A, gear B, and main gear,
and drives the optical pickup with the rack gear.
Gear A and gear B are double clutch gears.
The inner REST switch is closed by the optical pickup base when the optical pickup is returned to the in-
nermost position by the traverse mechanism.

section: CO-1 Traverse mechanism and optical pickup (1-1 traverse mech, 1-2 3-beam vs single beam, 1-3 t
text:
1-2 3-Beam Type and Single Beam Type
The optical pickup of the SL-XP7 is a single beam type instead of a 3-beam type. The structure of the
optical pickup is shown in Fig. 1-2.
The largest difference in optical structure between the 3-beam type and single beam type is that the single
beam type has no diffraction grating. Therefore, the single beam type has only beam on the optical path,
and its photo-detector is divided into four instead of six (four plus two).
The two sub-beams of the 3-beam type have the function of generating tracking errors. The process of
generating tracking errors by the single beam type that is without sub-beams is described in the following.
Focus errors are generated by the astigma method as in conventional models.

text:
1-3 Tracking Error Generation
Fig. 1-3 shows the basic configuration of the single beam type (phase difference detecting method).
The output of the optical pickup is the sum of each diagonal element of the 4-divided photo-detector.
Phase
difference
detector
Comparator Tracking error
(4-divided photo-detector)
Fig. 1-3 Basic Configuration
If a track pit image is assumed to pass over the 4-divided photo-detector, and deviates to the left or to the
right, a phase difference corresponding to the track deviation is generated between output signals (A1
+ A2) and (A3 + A4). This phase difference is detected by the phase detector, and passed through the
lowpass filter (L.P.F.) to generate a tracking error.

section: CO-5 Microcomputer peripheral circuits (5-1 reset, 5-2 keyboard interface, 5-3 LCD/LED display)
text:
LCD display
The LCD is used for track and time display.
Serial data synchronized with the clock is input from the microcomputer to the LCD driver, and each
time that serial data ends, LOAD signal is added to the data to be sent to the LCD.
OSC is a terminal for generating a COM frequency, which is one-eighth of the OSC frequency. Signal
voltage between COM and each SEG are used for LCD display as follows:
SEG output with phase opposite to COM signal: .............. ON
SEG output with same phase to COM signal............ 0000 OFF
LED display
The LED display indicates seven statuses.
Serial data synchronized with the clock is input from the microcomputer to the LED driver, and
each time that serial data ends, LATCH signal is added to the data for selecting an LED and giving
an indication. The two pilot lamps that are connected to 07 are orange and green and operate as
follows:
1) Orange pilot lamp lights when no disk is in.
2) Green pilot lamp lights when a disk is inserted.
3) Orange and green lamps alternately light during loading or ejection.

text:
6-2 Laser APC Circuit
Fig. 6-3 shows the laser APC circuit.
When a laser ON mode command is emitted, pin 5 goes high to turn the laser on.
A loop circuit is formed by O and D (the laser paired with a PIN diode) and the APC in the IC, and laser
beam intensity is detected by the PIN diode in APC operation.
lf laser beam intensity increases, the PIN diode’s photo-electric current increases so that the pin 10
voltage rises (pin 12 voltage is the reference voltage) to decrease laser beam intensity.

6-3. RF Amplifier and Dropout Detector Circuits
(1) RF amplifier circuit
RF signal is the total sum of the 4-divided photo-detector (A1 +A2 +A3 +AA4) of the optical pickup.
These are added in the optical pickup, and are input via Q to pin 33 . (Q is located in the optical
pickup.}
The output is taken out from pin 31, from which it is sent to the next IC for PLL (AN8371S).
The gain between pin 33 andpin 31 is about 34 dB.
(2) Dropout detector circuit
In dropout detection, a dropout on the disk is detected from the above-mentioned RF signal, the
tracking servo is stabilized, and its detection signal is output to pin 32.
The detecting process is shown in Fig. 6-5. The level goes high if a dropout is detected.
—23—

text:
Tracking error circuit
The tracking error circuit inputs the I-V converted signals to pins 2 and 4 via C119 and C117.
The comparators shape the waveforms.
In the tracking error process of the single beam type, the phase difference between the two signals
is detected and a pulse corresponding to the phase difference is generated as described in 2-3. Deviat-
ing direction is judged from the polarity of the pulse. The generated pulse is smoothed by the LPF
into an analog tracking error (TE) signal. This is how the phase comparator and LPF operate.
Then, the TE signal is output from pin 6 (TE OUT) via the TE amplifier and TE SW.
VR102 is the tracking gain (TR GAIN) control, and VR106 the tracking offset (TR OFFSET)
control.
Kick and hold circuits
Kick means jumping the beam from one track to another during a pause or manual search. Kick
timing is set by a control signal from the microcomputer, and a kick signal is output to pin 20. The
waveform of each kick signal is shown in Fig. 6-10.
The hold circuit holds the preceding value of a TE signal in a kick section. TE SW is kept off during a
kick. Signal waveforms during a pause kick are shown in Fig. 6-11.
—28—

Brake circuit
The brake circuit brakes the tracking actuator to quickly retracts the tracking servo after rapid feed
or kick (10/100).
The process is shown in Fig. 6-12.
The brake circuit applies a single limiter (indicated by the dotted line in the figure) to the TE signal
to absorb the energy after a kick.
The figure shows the case of KICK REV. In the case of KICK FWD, the brake is applied with the
single limiter inverted in polarity. Therefore, the brake circuit requires a kick direction discriminating
signal, which is generated from a tracking cross signal and off track signal as shown in Fig. 6-13.
The cross signal has an advanced phase in KICK FWD, and a delayed phase in KICK REV. Braking
direction is determined by detecting this phase difference.

12 samples of data (six each for the right and left) are taken as a frame for signal processing. In
other words, 24-symbol data constitutes a frame. W1 to W24 shown in Fig. 9-1 correspond to
it.
Data W1 to W24 are first scrambled by C2. Scramble may be considered to be a small interleave.
In C2 scramble, the data are delayed over two frames alternately in units of sample data.
After the C2 scramble, the data enter the C2 encoder, which generates 4-symbol parity signals
Q1 to Q4 from the 24-symbol data using reed solomon code, and arranges them in the frame
center.
The symbol data count in one frame is 28 in total.
Next is the interleave.
As shown in the figure, the interleave delays the 28-symbol data, including the Q parity signals,
over the range of 4 frames minimum to 108 frames maximum.
The C1 encoder generates 4-symbol parity signals P1 to P4 from the 28-symbol data, which
have been rearranged by interleaving, using reed solomon code, and arranges them at the frame
end.
Here, the symbol data count in a frame is 32 in total. (See Fig. 9-3.)

the next frame.
8) Control data P to W are otherwise called subcodes or users bits, containing time information
for random access or display and consisting of a single symbol (8 bits).
These signals are arranged at the head of a frame.
Entry of these control signals increases the symbol data count in a frame to 33 in total.
9) Finally, the above 1-frame data are EFM-modulated, a frame synchronizing signal is added, and
the data are recorded on the disk.
EFM modulation is described in detail in the next paragraph.
All these are intended for improving the correction capacity.
This system is called CIRK (Cross Interleave Reed Solomon Code).

EFM is a new modulation system for CD, and stands for Eight to Fourteenth Modulation meaning
modulating 8 symbol data bits to 14 channel bits.
EFM is necessary because the data bit arrangement of 1’s and O’s cannot be defined if symbol data
remains as such.
If 1’s or O’s continue so long, data will be a direct current so that self-clocks cannot be generated by
the tracking servo (using pits) and reproducing system.
Conversely, if 1’s and O’s are frequently reversed, it will be necessary to reduce the laser beam to a
very small diameter.

A reproducing system signal processing block diagram is shown in Fig. 9-8.
The flow of reproducing system signal processing is just opposite to the flow of recording system
signal processing. Here, decoders are error detection and correction are used in place of the C1 and
C2 encoders that are used for parity generation.
Both the C1 and C2 decoders are capable of error detection and correction. If data is incorrectable
in the C1 decoder, C1 flag is attached to that data, and after deinterleaving, the data is sent to the
C2 decoder for accurate correction.
If data is incorrectable in the C2 decoder, an average value is obtained from the preceding and next
data after C2 unscramble, followed by interpolation processing.

EFM demodulation, subcode demodulation
In EFM demodulation, an extraction clock PCK is used to latch EFM signal every 14 bits to
return it to the original 8-bit data.
The frame clock of 7.35 kHz in EFM signal is output from pin @ (CLDCK) by synchronized
detection.
In subcode demodulation, the sychronized signal in the 14 bits preceding EFM demodulation is
detected, and subcode Q data is output to pin @) (SUBQ) and emphasis/de-emphasis signal to pin
@) (DEMPHA) (high in case of emphasis signal).
Also, a subcode QO block clock of 75 Hz is output from pin 1 (BLKCK).
C1, C2 unscramble, deinterleave
Time base processing (data rearrangement) is used during recording to deal with various burst
errors and random errors that occur through the recording and reproducing systems.
The data thus rearranged is returned to the original state by an operation opposite to that of
recording, using an external RAM (16K).
(a) Pins 43 to 50 (DO to D7) : Data signals to RAM
(b) Pin 6) (RAM WE) : Command signal to write in RAM
(c) Pin 62 (RAM OE) : Command signal to read from RAM

For digital signal processing, data is once written in an external RAM and read out again. A
RAM address generator circuit is provided in the LSI for this purpose. Because a crystal clock
is used for reading data and a clock synchronized with reproducing signals (corresponding to
PCK). is used for writing data, however, address locations may be unsteady relative to RAM
capacity. The fine servo detects address location signals and operates to keep the read/write pace
constant.
Traverse tracking servo
The traverse tracking servo tracks the traverse position to keep linear velocity constant when
the traverse mechanism is in rapid feed.
This servo operates in such a way that two consecutive shortest period of SRF will be 6 times
the period of the reference clock 1T (4.3 MHz).
TRON is used for switching the traverse tracking servo to the 11T servo or vice versa. That is,
the traverse tracking servo is selected when TRON is high; the 11T servo is selected when TRON
is low.

10-1 D—A Converter
1C801 is a D—A converter, which converts
digital signals to analog signals. Digital signals
are input to pins 1 to 16 of 1C801, 16 bits
parallel. Pin 1 (B1) is MSB, and pin 16 (B16)
is LSB. PAM signal is output from pin 17
(OUT).
(Lch = 1 kHz, Rech = 0)

10-2 Deglitch Circuit
The deglitch circuit consists of 1C253 (analog switch), 1C252 (operational amplifier), C255 and C355 (for
hold).
Pin 19 (L DG) of 1C601 (LSI) is the deglitch signal output for the left channel, and pin 20 (R DG) of
1!C601 is the deglitch signal output for the right channel.
Fig. 10-3 shows a demodulation timing chart of the deglitch circuit.
When L DG signal is low, the left channel circuit takes signals in, while the right channel circuit outputs
the signals that have been taken in (and held by C255).

The lowpass filter (LPF) restores the signals containing harmonics (staircase waves) received from the
deglitch circuit to complete audio signals.
The LPF also has a de-emphasis function.
It reads emphasis or no emphasis from subcode (Q channel), and outputs a control signal from pin 21
(DEMPHA) of 1C601 (LSI). De-emphasis is applied when the output signal is high.

text:
Today,our music sources consist of FM/AM
tuners, recorded discs and tape.
Recently, a new source has been added on
PCM (pulse code modulation) technology.
The new source that is attracting is
1. Analog VS Digital
1-1. Quality
Analog recordings have undergone
remarkable improvements to data, but
they are still limited by distortion and
in dynamic range. Digital recording, on
the other hand, is a_ revolutionary
technique which eliminates these
limitations.
Digital disc typically have a flat
frequency response throughout the entire
audible frequency range of 20 through
20,000 Hz. Their wide dynamic range
exceeds 90dB, as the digital signal can
always be recovered and is identical to
the original signal. Totally different
from present analog turntable system,
the digital discs never exhibit
deterioration in sound reproduction
quality no matter how many times it is
played. Even more remarkably, they can
include flexible, convenient automatic
play and program search features that
were never possible with conventional
analog player designs.
1-2. Advantages of Optical System
a) Exceptional Durability
With the mechanical system as in the
current analog player system, the stylus
must be in physical with the disc.
Therefore both the stylus and the disc
will wear out after a certain period of
time, causing serious deterioration of
sound quality.
With the optical system, however , the

Therefore both the stylus and the disc
will wear out after a certain period of

With the optical system, however , the
lack of contact between the disc and the
pick-up means that there is no sonic

Digital Audio. This technical guide will

b) Harmful Effect of Dust and Scratches
Minimized
Mechanical and variable capacitance
system are easily affected by dust and
scratches, since signals are impressed
directly in the disc surface. The
compact disc, on the other hand, has a
Imm thick protective layer aver tha
signal pits. More importantly, the spot
size of the laser beam is only about 1mm
in diameter at the surface of the disc,
but is as small as lnm at the signal
layer. This means that a dust particle
or a scratch on the disc surface is
actually only a millionth in size on the
signal surface.

text:
3. Compact Disc Features
1) Superior Sound Features
To maintain master recorder quality,
the information on the disc is recorded
with 16 bits linear quantization.
To improve recording density (playback
time) eight to fourteen bits modulation
(EFM) is used. This allows 2. channel
playback for max 74 minutes.
To realize stable data reproduction a
special error correcting code called
the Cross Interleave Reed-Solomon Code
(CIRC) is used.
2) Virtually Indestructible
The non contact laser playback system
allows repeated use with no degradation
in quality.
The plastic coating over the signal
information protects it against
scratches, dirt and fingerprints.
3) Small Size
The small size allows for easy compact
strage (12cm and 8cm CD).
4) Random Access
The control information recorded on the
disc allows random access and character
display such as names of tunes, artists
etc.
4. PCM Features
Using a PCM system for audio
reproduction has certain advantages.
1)Not affected by noise of the recording
medium, The digital system only has
detect two types of signals (0 and 1).
This is much easier than trying to
detect the infinite number of possible
amplitudes and frequencies of an
analog signal.
2)Eliminates effects of uneven rotation
of the playback equipment due to a
quartz controlled reading clock.
3)Able to correct errors, besides
including the recorded signal, the

analog signal.
2)Eliminates effects of uneven rotation
of the playback equipment due to a
quartz controlled reading clock.
3)Able to correct errors, besides
including the recorded signal, the
digital data has error correction
information. This allows the digital
circuit to calculate what the
information should be if the music
signal can not be rear properly
because the disc surface is marked by
dirt or scratches etc.
5. PCM Process for CD
The PCM process has several fundamental
steps regardless of whether the
application is satelite data
transmission or simply audio
reproduction etc. A general description
is given of the recording and playback
procedures followed by an explanation of
each steps.
6. Disc Mastering
6-1 Campact Disc Cutting
In a Compact Disc Cutting System, the
Digital Audio signal is sent through a
CIRC encording modulator unit. In this
way, EFM modulation is performed and
control and sync bits are added. The
modulated signal is then sent to a laser
cutter to produce the metal master.
The cutting of the metal master is not
really a burning of the layer by the
laser. In figure 6-1 the real cutting is
represented.

smoothness of the surface.

8-1 Lead-in and Lead-out Signals
The lead-in signal is located just in
front of where the signal area starts,
while the lead-out signals appears right
after the end of the signal area. These
two signals are used to control the
movement of the optical pick-up.
8-2 Table of Contents (TOC)
Written in the lead-in area is the time
information on control codes including
the start time of each selection as well
as the total number and playing time of
selections, which can be read out before
performance starts for the convenience
of program search and so on. Such
information can also be displayed.
8-3 Control Codes
These codes distinguish between 2-
channel recording and 4—channel
recording. They can also detect whether
preemphasis is given to a particular
recording. Furthermore, they can even
change the circuit connections of the
player automatically according to the
detected conditions of the disc.
| 8-4 Music Start Flag
The music start flag is provided in the
blank space between selections. By
counting this flag, therefore it is
possible to locate any desired selection
on the disc. Even when the end of a
selection fades in to the beginning of
the next, the flag can be inserted a
minimum of two seconds in front of the
second selection so that such selections
can be recognized not as a single piece
of music but as two separate selections.
8-5 Track Number and Index

8-5 Track Number and Index
Selections recorded on the disc can be
numbered from 1 to 99. Each bar in a
piece of music can also be addressed up
to 99.
With the time code function, you can
tell the time lapse from the beginning
of each slection in minutes, seconds,
and 1/75 of a second. During the blank
Space between selections, the time is
counted down.
As exemplified above, the control bits
can be used in a variety of ways. They
not only let you locate any portion of
music exactly and quickly but also allow
random playback in any order you set.
And despite the long playing time of an
hour on one side, access to the desired
point can be achieved almost instantly.
This is one of the greatest advantages
of the CD system which cannot be found
in any other system.
9. Analog Signal Versus Digital Signal
An analog signal is a continuous signal
in two respects: value and time.
A digital signal is discrete, both in
value and in time. Discrete in time
means that the signal is defined on
discrete intervals of time. Discrete in
value means that the signal has finite
number of possible values.
A digital signal is a sequence of words,
each representing the value of a sample.
The value of a word or digital signal,

. Discrete in
value means that the signal has finite
number of possible values.
A digital signal is a sequence of words,
each representing the value of a sample.
The value of a word or digital signal,
the binary code, is a combination of "1"
(on) and "0" (off). The composing parts
of the binary code are the bits.
Bit is an abbreviation for "binary
digit". It is the smallest unit that can
have a meaning in binary notation, and
that can only have two values, "ON" or
"OFF", represented as "1" or "0".
The higher the number of bits used in
the binary code, the higher the
resolution and the combination of bits,
which means the higher the accuracy to
describe the value of the sample.

the sampling frequency is at least

present in the input signal.
This is the famous Nyquist criterion on

or shannon theorem).
Since the highest frequency found in an
audio signal is approximately 20KHz, and
as selecting an unnecessary high
sampling frequency would increase both
complexity and cost of the conversion
circuitry, a frequency of 44.1KHz has
been chosen as the standard for the
compact disc.

10-2 Sample Hold Circuit
In the practice of analog to digital
conversion, the sampling operation is
performed by so called sample hold
circuit which, once the sample has been
taken, store the sample analog voltage
for the time during which it can be
converted into a digital code by the A/D
converter, The principle of the sample
hold circuit is relatively simple.
A basic sample hold circuit is in fact a
voltage .memory device that stores a
given voltage in a high-quality
capacitor. To sample the input voltage,
switch S closes momentarily; when §
opens, capacitor C holds the voltage
until S closes again and passes the next
sample, see figure 10-5,
Figure 10-5 Basic Sample-Hold Principle
The sample hold circuit are not only
used in A/D conversion to sample an
analog input signal, but also in the
reverse stage, after the D/A conversion,
to remove transients from the output of
the D/A converter and thus facilitate
the task of the low pass filter. In this
case, it is often called deglitcher.
10-3 Filtering
In the foregoing, we have seen that low
pass filtering is required at two places
in a digital audio system:
1) During recording, in the A/D stage
before the input sampler, we need
an anti-aliasing filter that
drastically suppresses all input
frequencies higher than the Nyquist
frequency.
2) During playback, i.e. in the compact
disc player, we need a
reconstruction filter after the

title: Technical Guide CD Player Technology SL-P150/SL-P405C (AD8812333T0)
section: 10 Analog to digital conversion (sampling, quantization)
text:
anti-aliasing filter that
drastically suppresses all input
frequencies higher than the Nyquist
frequency.
2) During playback, i.e. in the compact
disc player, we need a
reconstruction filter after the
sample hold in the D/A stage to
separate the sample audio signal
from its images sround the harmonics
of the sampling frequency.
Consequently, both filters must be very
linear within the passband, and have a
very high rejection out of it; this will
unavoidably bring along phase and group
delay distortions within the audio
passband as well as ripple and ringing.
Apart from that, the noise and THD
performance of these filters has to be
better than the limits posed by the
quantization process itself. In practice
this means that 100dB S/N ratio have to
be attained.
For the practical realization of such
low pass filter, there are serveral
approaches possible:
1) Passive Filter:
7th to 9th order filters must be used
to obtain the required rejection. The
coils which must be used give
problemss because of non-linearity,
size andcost. Noise, however, is
hardly a problem in this type of
filters.
2) Active Filter:
Can also be used but the
specifications are more stringent
than usually encountered with active-
filter designs; therefore, a very
careful design is necessary. The
distortion can be made better than
with passive filters, but the noise
worse.

3) Digital Filter:
Digital filter techniques allow to
design almost ideal characteristics
with relative ease. Their use for
digital audio coding, however,
implements an increased complexity of
the related circuitry (initial gentle
analog filtering with linear phase
response followed by conversion and
then digital filtering).
In practical CD players, active analog
filters are used in most _ players;
however, the latest generation deck
players use digital filters combined
with an oversampling D/A conversion
circuit.

in fact, quantization can be regarded as
a mechanism in which some information is
thrown away, keeping only as much as is
required to retain a certain accuracy as
is needed in a certain application.
By definition, since all voltages in a

creates anerror, called quantization
error.
This error can be perceived s a kind of
noise, and therefore the quantization
error is also called quantization noise.
It is clear that, the smaller the
quantization intervals, the smaller this
quantization noise will be.

13. Error Correction Basics
1. Nature and Causes of Code Error
The error correction scheme iS an
essential part of the CD system. With
analog techniques, the effort of error
such as dropouts is that the sound is
merely skipped, and the listener may not
hear it, unless he is very attentive.
However, with digital audio, the
dropouts are heard in the form of
irritating pulse noise.
Roughly categorized, there are two types
of code error:
a) The first type are random error,
caused in disc production by
inaccurate photo-resist coating,
cutting, microscope bubbles, etc.
b) The second type are the burst error
resulting from scratches, dust and
fingerprints on the disc surface;
when these error occur, some bits or
even bytes may be missing, this means
dropouts are produced and this leads
to critical reabout error in the
digital data.
2. Error Detection
First of all, it is necessary to detect
whether there is a code error. The error
detection code is used for this purpose:
extra bits are added to the data bits
under certain rules, and then, by

The information on the CD is contained
in the ca. 20000 tracks, whereas each
track is subdivided in frames. The
"framerate"equals 7350 Hz, which means
that every second, 7350 of these frames
are processed in the CD player. After

The each frame holds 8 bits of subcode
information, this means the subcode area
of CD stores 211,680,000 data bits ( ca.
200 Megabits).
The 8 bits of the subcode word are used
for 8 different subcode channels (P, Q,
R, S, TT, U, V and W). Presently, only
channel P and channel Q are defined. The
content and the format of the channels
R, S, T, V and W is still under
discussion.
The 8 bits of the subcode word have no
meaning at the frame level, Only when a
block of 98 frames is read by the
player, the 8 subcode channels (98 bits
each) get a specific content. The
content of the channels is refreshed on
updated for each new block of 98 frames
( or 75 times a second).

15. Calculation of the Different Bit Rates
1. Analog to Digital Conversion
Fs = 44.000 KHz
q = 16 bits
n = 2 Channels
Bits Rate = Fs x q x n = 1.411200 MHz
2. CIRC Encoding
6 words (of 16 bits) of the L-channel
A/D converter and 6 words (of 16 bits)
of the R-channel A/D converter are fed
to the "C2" encoder. These 12 words of
16 bits are broken into 24 words of 8
bits. This is the input of the encoder
The "C2" encoder adds 4 words of 8
bits, and its output is 28 words of 8
bits. The :C2" encoder is called a
(24, 28) encoder. and The "C1" encoder
receives these 28 words at the input
and adds again 4 words of 8 bits. Its
output is 32 words of 8 bits and the
"C1" encoder is called a (28, 32)
encoder.
The extra words ( 8 words x 8 bit = 64
bits ) are called redundant words and
are used for the error correction.
The new bit rate now equals:
1.411200 x 32/24 = 1.881600 MHz
3. The Control Word
One control word ( 1 word x 8 bits) is
added to every 32 words of the
encoder.
The new bit rate becomes:
1.881600 x 33/32 = 1.940400 MHz
4. EFM Encoeding
Every word of 8 bits is replaced by a
"symbol" of 14 bits. To thaca 14 bite
3 extra junction bits are added. The
resultant operation transforms 8 data
bits into 17 (14 + 3) channel bits.
The new bit rate is:
1.940400 x 17/8 = 4.123350 MHz

16. Optical Pickup
1. Basic Operation of the Laser Diode
The basic operation of any laser
consists of pumping the atoms into a
stimulated state from which the
electrons can escape and fall to the
lower energy ground state by giving up a
photo of the appropriate energy. In a
solid-state laser such as the laser
diodes used in CD player, this principle
is applied to a PN-junction, as will be
explained below.
First, let us review the energy band
diagrams as shows figure 16-1.

As is commonly known, the energy state
of electrons falls within a certain
range or energy band.
The energy bands required for electrical
conductivity are:
(a)The "valency band", indicating the
energy level of the valency electron
and:
(b)The "conduction band", indicating the
energy level of the free electron.
In a metal, the valency band and
conduction band overlap each other in
part, so that the valency electron can
enter the conduction band and move
freely, which causes conductivity.
In a semiconductor or insulator, there
is an energy gap between the valency
band and the conduction band; this band
is called the forbidden band. In case of

In a semiconductor or insulator, there
is an energy gap between the valency

is called the forbidden band. In case of
an insulator, the forbidden or energy
gap "Eg" is large.
For a semiconductor, the energy gap is
rather small, so that it can become a
conductor by applying some external
energy.
P-type and N-type semiconductors can be
made by inserting impurities into the
semiconductor crystal. In the P-type
semiconductor, positive holes are
generated, which can move freely within
the valency band, and in the N-type
semiconductor, electrons are generated
which can move freely in the conduction
band.
If both types of semiconductors are
combined into one crystal, i.e. in a PN
junction, a natural electrical field is
created in this PN-junction section, but
the free electrons and positive holes
are kept in the respective areas, and do
not move to the other area, as they do
not have enough energy to cross the Eg
level. However, by applying energy from
outside, e.g. a voltage or current, to
the PN junction, the electrons and
positive holes start moving into the
other area as showns figure 16-2. Asa
result, electrons and positive holes,
coexisting in the PN junction, are now
recombined, and natural light is
emitted.

The principle of the injection iaser
diode as shows figure 16-3. The natural
light emitted due to the recombination
of the electrons and positive holes is
caught between two mirror plates; so
photons can excite other photons, by
injecting their light energy in the PN
junction, thus creating more electrons
and positive holes etc.

The light generated by recombination is
caught between the mirror side plates,
causes spontaneous emission, is
amplified and starts laser oscillation.
This stimulated emission can be so rapid
as to represent nearly an avalanche,
completely draining the high-energy
states in a subnanosecond burst of very
great energy.
On the other hand, certain types of
lasers can be produced which will
operate in an equilibrium condition,
giving up photons at just the input
energy pumping rate. The injection laser
diode operates in this mode.
The material in an injection laser dicde
is rather heavily doped so that, under
forward bias, The region near the
junction has a very high concentration
of holes an electrons. This produces the
inversion condition with a _ large
population of electrons in a high-energy

section: 16 Optical pick-up: laser diode, opto-electronics, single beam system, focus lens, focus/trac
text:
hat, under
forward bias, The region near the
junction has a very high concentration
of holes an electrons. This produces the
inversion condition with a _ large
population of electrons in a high-energy
band and a large population of holes in
the low-energy band.
In this condition, the stimulated
emission of photons can overcome the
photon absorption and a net light flux
will result. In operation, the forward
current must reach some threshold, to
achieve lasing operation. Just beyond
this threshold, the Laser operates with
a single "thread" of light, and the
output is relatively stable but low.
As the current is increased, the light
output climbs extremely rapidly. The
light output is highly temperature
sensitive. A small current variation or
modest temperature change can cause the
output to rise so rapidly that it
destroys the chip.
A photodiode, monitoring the light
output, is commonly used in a feedback
loop to overcome this problem. Like the
LED, the ILD must be driven from a
current source, rather thana voltage
source as the unit can go into thermal
runaway.
As a device begins to draw current, the
junction begins to warm and forward drop
decreases, which tends to drive the
voltage higher and in turn decrease the
foeward drop until the current tends
toward infinity and the device is
destroyed.
In addition, the ILD has a tendency to
deterioration with operation, and this

In addition, the ILD has a tendency to

text:

What is a Linear Velocity?
The compact disc uses a constant linear
veloocity (CLV) drive system. This means
that the disc speed changes to maintain
a constant reading speed approx 1.3 m/s.
In figure 17-1. shows the distance from
A to B is shorter than from C to D.
To read this data at a constant speed
the disc must rotate slower at the outer
periphery. The range is 500 rpm through
200 rpm from inner to outer periphery.
The proper speed is maintained by
reading the synchronizing signal
(7.35KHz) and comparing it to a
reference signal.
As pointed out before, the data on the
disc is recorded in blocks, which we
called "frame". Each frame starts with a
unique sync word, which is used to
cntrol the spindle motor.
The frequency of these sync words is
compared against a fixed frequency
(derived from a crystal oscillator) ina
phase comparator and the motor is driven
according to any frequency or phase
difference.

title: Technical Guide CD Player Technology SL-P150/SL-P405C (AD8812333T0)
section: 17.8-10 Traverse servo(60), linear motor(61-62), spindle CLV servo(63-65)
text:
As the length of the tracks increases
linearly from the linner (lead-in) track
to the outer (lead-out) track, the
number of frames per track increases in
the same respect. This means that the
frequency of the sync words’ also
increases, which causes the motor speed
to decrease, resulting in a constant
linear velocity. The angular velocity
typically decreases from 500 RPM (lead-
in track) to 200 RPM (lead-out track).
A run-up circuit is activated when the
disc is initially located to set the
motor speed at about 500 RPM. This makes
it possible to read the sync words and
hence to enable the servo circuit.
(1) Correlation with IC-301, IC—401,ICc-501
The CLV servo circuit controls disc
rotation to a constant linear velocity.
It includes three servo modes, i.e. CVL

15) Description of Modified Servo Circuit
(MN8373S and MN8374S)
1. General
The servo circuit in CD player with the
standard mechanism (SL-P150, SL-P200,
SL-P250, etc) has been entirely modified
during production. The units containing
modified servo circuit can be identified
as follows:
(1). Serial number suffix: Refer to

ORIGINAL DESIGN HAS BEEN CHANGED.
2. Circuit Configuration
The Servo circuit used in the
conventional FF-1 CD players comprised a
servo IC (AN8370S) and discrete circuit.
In contrast, the modified servo circuit
consists of three IC chips with on
discrete circuit.
(1). IC-101 (servo amprifier)
=Processes analog servo signals.
(2). IC-102 (servo controller)
=Processes digital servo signals.
(3). IC-103 (servo driver)
=Drives the focus,
traverse coils.
The block diagram of IC-101 (AN8373S) and
IC-102 (AN8374S) are shows figure 17-33.

the basic circuit configurations and
Operations are almost identical to those

the exception of the following details:
PLL adjustment eliminated

pulled into the PLL lock range by
using the CLK (88.2KHz) signal.

5. Data Signal Flow
(1). RF Signal Flow
* The photo detectors Al - A6 output
is applied to IC-101's RF IN INPUT
(pin 39) via an RF amplifier
within the Optical Pick-up.
* After being amplified by another
RF amplifier within IC-101, the
signal passes through an equalizer
for 3T compensation, goes into the
AGC (Auto Gain Control) circuit
where it undergoes automatic gain
control, and appears at the ARF
(RF signal controled by auto gain
control) output (pin 35) of
Ic-101.
(2). EFM Data Generation
* The RF signal applied to ICc-102's
ARF input (pin 12) is sliced by
the DSL (data sliced) into a pulse
signal EFM (eight to fourteen bit
modulation), and then coupled to
the PLL circuit.
* The PLL is synchronized with the
EFM signal and then coupled to the
signal processing block.
6. PL, Operations

The PLL circuit shows figure 17-35.

7. Control Logic (IC-102)
Commands used to set the servo circuit
status are supplied from the system
CPU in parallel 4 bit data (CNT1 -
CNT4).
SENSE is the status read signal for
Ic-102, which is transferred to the
system CPU. All other control logic
Operations are identical to those of
the conventional control logic.
8. Focus Servo Circuit Operation
(1). The outputs of the photo detector
are coupled to pin 2 - 5 of
Ic-101, where they are phase
corrected by the Al + A2 and A3 +
A4 signals and converted from
current to voltage signals. They
are transferred to the focus
balance circuit and subjected to
photo detector position error
correction by means of VR101
(best eye adjustment).
(2). The difference between the Al +
A2 and A3 + A4 signals, produced
within the FE mixing circuit,
serves as the Focus Error signal
which appears at IC-101 pin 15.
The signal is then applied to
Ic-102 pin 8. VR105 is used for
offset voltage injection control.
(3). Since the Focus switch is closed
in the PLAY mode, the FE signal
appears at 1C-102 pin 9 and
couples to the loop filter within
Ic-101, where it is used to

offset voltage injection control.
(3). Since the Focus switch is closed
in the PLAY mode, the FE signal
appears at 1C-102 pin 9 and
couples to the loop filter within
Ic-101, where it is used to
determine the focus. servo's
frequency response. The output of
the loop filter at IC-101 pin 23,
is transferred to the focus
driving circuit and drives the
focus actuator.

title: Technical Guide CD Player Technology SL-P150/SL-P405C (AD8812333T0)
section: 17.15 Modified servo circuit (AN8373S servo amp, MN8374S/AN8374S servo controller, servo driver)
text:
9. Tracking Servo Circuit Operation
(1). The focus balance circuit output,
Al + A2 and A3 + A4, are also
transferred to the tracking
balance circuit. The output of
the tracking balance circuit are
applied to the phase difference
limiter within IC-102, where they
are phase compared to produce a
tracking error signal.
The tracking error signal at
IC-102 pin 4 is subjected to gain
adjustment, then applied to the
loop filter, within Ic-101 via
the tracking switch.
. The loop filter output appearing
at IC-102 pin 22, is coupled to
pin 42 (BR IN/ tracking error
input) of IC-102, where it is fed
into a braking circuit. The
output of the braking circuit
appears at pin 41 (BR OUT/
tracking drive control signal)
and couples to the tracking coil
driver to drive the tracking
actuator's.
10. Traverse Servo Circuit. Operation
(1). PLAY mode:
The tracking error signal applied
to IC-102 pin 42 goes through the
traverse switch and TRV (traverse
circuit) filter (for response
compensation) and appears at pin
39. This output is used to
control the traverse actuator.
(2). KICK mode:
The KICK signal. decoded from the
system CPU command by the control
logic, appears at pin 27. It is
used to control the tracking
actuator which KICKs the pick-up
by a span of 1, 10, or 100 tracks
according to the system CPU
command.
Forced traverse mode:
The TRVF, TRVR signals supplied
from system CPU to pins 34 and

section: 17.15 Modified servo circuit (AN8373S servo amp, MN8374S/AN8374S servo controller, servo driver)
text:

actuator which KICKs the pick-up
by a span of 1, 10, or 100 tracks
according to the system CPU
command.
Forced traverse mode:
The TRVF, TRVR signals supplied
from system CPU to pins 34 and
35, respectively, are decoded to
produce a traverse drive signal.
The signal appears at pin 25 and
drives the traverse coil.
(4). Speed sensor operation:
The varying voltage output of the
potentionmeter connected to
IC-101 pin 30, is differentiated
by the circuit at pin 27 to 29
and fed into the traverse coil.
Smooth traverse action is
achieved by feeding back a
control signal which reflects the
traverse movements of the optical
pick-up. (The potentionmeter
yields a negative potential when
the optical pick-up moves
outward).
11. RF Signal Detection and Auto Focus
Circuit
The auto focus circuit within IC-102
performs focus search. If it detects an
FE signal S-Curve it closes the focus
switch contacts to close the focus servo
loop. At this point the RF detector .
within IC-101 detects the RF signal and
supplies it to the F.LOCK DET. input at
IC-102 pin 36.
The F.LOCK signal is used to indicate to
system CPU that focus is "IN". If focus
goes "OUT" and the RF signal is no longer
detected, the auto focus circuit opens
the focus loop switch and starts focus
search again.
12. Dropout Detection Circuit
(1). Black Band Dropout (BDO)
Dropouts are detected from the RF

section: 17.15 Modified servo circuit (AN8373S servo amp, MN8374S/AN8374S servo controller, servo driver)
text:

detected, the auto focus circuit opens
the focus loop switch and starts focus
search again.
12. Dropout Detection Circuit
(1). Black Band Dropout (BDO)
Dropouts are detected from the RF
signal within IC-101. In order to
stabilize the tracking servo against
dropout, the BDO signal is supplied
from IC-102 pin 37 to the phase
difference limitter and used to hold

The PCK (bit period clock= 4.3218 MHz)
is used to time signal processings
during 16K RAM write. RAM read and
subsequent operations are timed by a
clock which is a derived from the
crystal-controlled master clock,
The jitter contained in the play signal
is absorbed by the RAM. The basic
internal operations of the digital
processing circuit are explained on the
following pages.
1) EFM Demodulation
(1)Sync signal detectio, protection, and
interpolation:
The EFM signal read off the disc (under
optical system servo control) is coupled
to the data slice/clock sampling
circuit, where it is converted into a
logic-level signal, separated into the
EFM and PCK signals, and applied to the
EFM demodulator.
The input EFM signal is first converted
into NZRZI data (inverted for every one;
non-inverted for every zero), then is
applied to a 24 bits shift register,
where the sync, signal is extracted from
the data.
Interpolation is required to cope with
sync, Signal dropout or pseudo sync,
signal generated due to defects on the
disc. In order to prevent the
synchronization system being disturbed
by the pseudo sync, signal a small sync.
Detection window is provided each time
the sync, signal should be found, so
that sync detection is performed only
within the window.
If no sync signal is detected in the
window, interpolation is done by an
internal 588 increment counter (which

section: 18 Digital circuit MN6617: block (76), EFM demod(77), subcode(78), interpolation & D/A interf
text:
sync, signal should be found, so
that sync detection is performed only
within the window.
If no sync signal is detected in the
window, interpolation is done by an
internal 588 increment counter (which
counts 588 PCK pulses). Also the number
of sync detection failures is counted,
and the width of the detection window is
automatically controlled according to
the count value.
The FCLV signal status changes depending
on whether the sync signal has been
detected or not:
*In every frame where on sync signal was
detected, the FCLV is set low.
—77—
*In every frame where the sync signal
was detected, the FCLV is set
high. (the sync detection failure
counter is reset at a high transition
of the FCLV)
If no sync signal has been detected for
eight consecutive frames, it is
considered an off-synchronization. The
RESY output of the device is set low,
which fully opens the window to attempt
synchronization:
**If a step out occurred, the RESY is
set low.
**When the device attempts a
synchronization, the RESY is set high.
The MN6617 can use the TRON (tracking
on) signal for external synchronization
control. When the tracking servo is off
(TRON = high), the device always fully
opens the window, so that it is ready
for synchronization as soon as_ the
tracking servo is turned on:
**When tracking servo is on, TRON is set
low.
**When tracking servo is off, TRON is
set high.

The device inputs the demodulated data
from the subcode-block and sync signals

The BLKCK signal indicating the block

(2) CRC check on Q data
Q data is subjected to CRC check, and
the check result is output to the CRC
and STAT pins of the device.
If an error is detected, both CRC and
STAT are set high, if no CRC error is
detected, both CRC and STAT are set low.
When the TRON input is high, the CRC
check result output are forced high.
(3) P to W data
The 8 bits data, (P, Q, R, S, T, U, V,
and W) are subjected to subcode
demodulation and loaded into an 8 bits
parallel to serial register at the CLDCK
timing. It is then shifted out in series
through the SUBC pin at an external SBCK
shift clock timing.
(4) De-emphasis detection
The device extracts one bit, which
indicates if emphasis is on or off from
the Q data and supplies it to the DEMPH
pin. De-emphasis is on when the DEMPH is
high. To suppress rapid output
transistions, the DEMPH output holds the
previous state if a CRC error has’ been
detected.

The MN6617 accesses the external 16K
byte RAM for the following read and
write functions of the modulated EFM

** Cl unscramble
** Deinterleave
** C2 unscramble
**kError correction flags
To make these RAM accesses efficient,
the RAM address controller assigns
different levels of priority to RAM
access. The level of priority is
identified by the interrupt acknowledge
logic so that the relevant address is
supplied to RAM.
Each frame contains 2304 clocks of XCK
(16.9344 MHz), and every RAM access
cycle requires 12 XCK clocks (709 ns).
So each frame contains up to 192 access
slots.
(1) RAM address generation
The effective addresses for the 16K byte
SRAM (static RAM) are given by an 11
bits read frame counter and an 11 bits
write frame counter. The read frame
counter is incremented by a crystal
controlled frame clock. The write frame
counter is incremented each time one
frame (32 symbols) of EFM data is
written into the RAM,

(2) Jitter absorption and RAM address
reset
The demodulated EFM data is synchronous
with the PCK signal produced by the
clock extraction logic and contains disc
wow and flutter components that cause
signal jitter. In order to eliminate
this jitter, the EFM data is written
into the 16K byte S-RAM, then read out
of it at acrystal controlled clock
timing.
The mragin for jitter is 13 frames. If
the difference between the contents of
the 11 bits read and write frame
counters exceeds +4 frames, a RAM
address reset occurs, and the write
frame counter value is loaded into the
read frame counter (at the dame time
FLAG 6 is set).
For a forced RAM address reset, the
device uses the TRON signal. This
enables each track access to have the
maximum jitter margin.

The error correction logic provides Cl-

for the interpolation. The interpolation
logic selects the type of the Cl flag
according to C2 flag, and provides
interpolation only for the symbol for
which the Cl flag is set.

1) Principle of the Digital Filter
The way an audio wave is converted to a
digital signal, processed digitally, and
then returned toa high-purity audio
form, is more and more widely
understood.
The conversion from analogue into
digital signals is often called pulse
code modulation, or PCM. The analogue
waveform is first sampled (measured at
regular intervals). Then it is
quantized. This means that it is given
the nearest numerical value in the large
range of numbers used to transmit the
digital sound information. The quantized
value is then converted to binary form
and encoded into a pulse train
representing the series of numbers. This
process of analogue to digital
conversion is shows in figure 19-1.

The pulse train is fed into’ the

reception or playback end, the pulse

regenerated in analogue form in the
reverse process known as digital to

2) How the Number of Bits Affects S/N
The accuracy of a digital system depends
on the number of bits used for the
binary number. This is because the
number of bits determines the accuracy
with which the samples taken from the
original waveform can be quantized, i.e.
expressed in digital form.
Two bits give four 2 possible values for
use in quantization, also three bits
give eight 2 possible values.
Every bit added doubles the number of
possible values. In audio terms, this
adds 6dB to the signal to noise ratio,
because it reduces the quantization
noise by a factor of 2.
The sixteen bits as used in the CD
system give 65536 (216 ) possible values
for quantization, anda signal to noise
ratio of 96dB. The audio signals are
encoded in the actual CD with this
ratio.
96dB is approximation. An additional
factor, which depends on the type of
signal, is always present, regardless of
the number of bits; for sine wave
signals this makes the theoretical
figure 97.8dB.

3) The Effect of the Sampling
Frequency
Another important factor is sampling
frequency, for efficiency in digital
operations, this is kept low (44.1KHz)
at a little over twice the maximum audio
frequency (20.0KHz). During the sampling
process this frequency and its harmonics
or multiples become modulated with the
original waveform in a series of
frequency bands as shows figure 19-2.
The bottom end of the lowest band is
rather close to the top of the audio
frequency range.
Figure 19-2
Figure 19-2 shows the frequency spectrum
produced by sampling showing’ the
periodic repetitions of the audio band.
The bottom end of the lowest band is
close to the audio frequency range.
4) Quantization Noise
In a digital audio system the audible
noise has a different character to the
familiar noise in an analogue audio
system. The digital audio system
background noise is called quantization
noise.
The quantization noise of a system can
be defined as the error signal between
the original waveform before the
analogue to digital conversion process,
and the restored waveform after the
digital to analogue conversion process.
This error signal can be considered as
both noise and distortion at the same
time.
Figure 19-3
Figure 19-3 shows the quantization
noise, The difference between the
original audio waveform = and the
regenerated wave after D/A conversion
(a) causes quantization noise (b).

The 16 bits analogue to digital

delivers a 16 bits digital signal with
an intrinsic accuracy or signal to noise

An ideal digital to analogue converter
(D/A) would deliver an analogue output
signal without adding noise to it.
However, ideal D/A do not exist a small
but finite electronic inaccuracy adds
noise to the quantization noise of the
digital signal.
The inaccuracy of a 16 bits D/A (the
resolution limit of half the least
significant bit) can be interpreted as a
noise source that reduces the signal to
noise ratio of the D/A to 96dB.

21. CD Changer’s Operation
This section explains the SI,P405C CD
changer's mechanism operation's and
mechanism logic control operations
(including SL-P400C etc).
[Se 7
The SL-P405C incorporates a
recently-developed disc loading unit with
an elevating mechanism which enables the
user to load up to six compact discs in a
magazine and play them in the desired
sequence. The SL-P405C uses the One Beam
system (FF-1MK2) for its optical (laser)
pick-up.
The disc magazine allows loading and
unloading of individual discs. The disc
detection mechanism (provided only on
selected models) provides disc search and
displays the presence of discs on the
player's display.
The mechanism section uses three DC
motors for: Disc Loading, Elevator, and
the Spindle. These motors are controlled
by the system CPU (ICc-401).
The SL-P405Cc signal processing logic and
audio circuit are almost identical to
those used in our comparable CD players.

basic sections: The magazine holder, the
Disc Loader, and the Optical Deck. See

text:
| 3-2. Disc Loading Operation
After the magazine has been loaded, the
elevator unit remains in the "standby"
mode, until a disc is selected. The
following example will describe the
operation sequence to select the third
disc and play it shows figure 21-12.
(1). Magazine
operation:
loading to standby
The magazine is inserted and the
unit enters the "standby" mode as
described in the previous section.
(2). Disc loading operation:
When "Disc 3" is selected, the CPU
(Ic-401) energizes the elevation
motor to lift the disc loader. At
this time the elevator gear
generates two pulses per rotation.
The CPU monitors the rising edge of
the height sensor (D451) signal.
The disc loader elevates from one
disc to the next each time the CPU
detects a complete rotation. When
the CPU detects the target pulse
(Target - 1/2), it issues a command
to reduce the supply voltage to the
elevator motor (slow lift command).
At the target disc the CPU shuts off
the elevator motor current.
Disc tray "pull-out" sequence:
The loading motor is energized to
pull out the third disc tray. When
the CPU detects that the draw switch
(S453) is closed, it reduces the
supply voltage to the loading motor.
When the CPU subsequently detects
that the loading switch (S452) is
closed, it shuts off the loading
motor current.
. Disc clamp operation:
Since the optical deck is located
two disc span below the first disc,

title: Technical Guide CD Player Technology SL-P150/SL-P405C (AD8812333T0)
section: 21 CD changer operation (magazine, elevator, timing charts, problem solving, apparent faults,
text:
CPU subsequently detects
that the loading switch (S452) is
closed, it shuts off the loading
motor current.
. Disc clamp operation:
Since the optical deck is located
two disc span below the first disc,
the loading units must be lowered to
the C (clamp) position. To do this,
the CPU energizes the elevator motor
so that it will lower the disc
loader. This time, the CPU counts
the falling edge of the height
sensor pulses. When the CPU counts 8
pulses, it brakes the elevation
motor, and when it detects the
falling edge of the 9th pulse, it
stops the motor.
Play operation:
The disc clamper secures the disc on
the turntable and the optical deck
starts playing the disc.

4. Height Adjustment of the Elevator
Unit
At rest (standby) position, the elevator
unit must be positioned 1.6mm above the
magazine holder surface.
The purpose of this adjustment is to set
this relative position. When performing
this adjustment, the shutter is adjusted
so that the pulse count (generated by the
photo detector and detected by the CPU)
corresponds to the proper height. If the

—ZbE—
6 Apparent Fault
The changer’s auto changing system may exhibit the following malfunctions but they may not be
derived from mechanism or logic failure:
Program numbers which do not exist
on the discs can be programmed in
the Program mode but nothing is
played in Play mode. (e.g. the
25th track was programmed for a
CD containing only 12 tracks.)
Disc trays were loaded only in
slots 1, 2, and 5 in the disc
magazine, and the player was
turned off when it was playing
Disk 5. When the player was
subsequently turned on, Disc 5 was
returned to the tray for Disk 3
(disk position has changed in
the magazine).
Possible cause
Other CD players first read the TOC just after a disc is loaded, th*n enter the
Pause mode to wait for the next command. They can verify the valid-ty of the
programmed contents by comparing the number of tracks on the disc wth that in
the program. However, the SL-P600C takes so much time to read the [OCs on all
of the six discs that it ignores invalid track numbers in the progrim,
As long as the player is left turned on, the CPU memorizes which slot the disc
now on the playing deck came from. However, once the player has been turned
off, the CPU loses its memory and cannot determine to which slot the disc
should be returned. In such a case, the CPU sequentially searches for a vacant

title: Technical Guide CD Player Technology SL-P150/SL-P405C (AD8812333T0)
section: 21 CD changer operation (magazine, elevator, timing charts, problem solving, apparent faults,
text:
from. However, once the player has been turned
off, the CPU loses its memory and cannot determine to which slot the disc
should be returned. In such a case, the CPU sequentially searches for a vacant
slot from bottom to top, and returns the disc into the first vacant Slot found.
At an occupied slot, the Load switch remains off. The CPU checks the time
until the Load switch is turned on after a return sequence was started (Draw
switch S453 was turned off). If it is too long (more than ms), the CPU
identifies that the slot is occupied.
* This problem can be avoided if all of the six trays are always loaded in the
magazine (discs need not be loaded in all of the six slots), or if trays are
loaded from slot 1 with no intermediate vacant slot left in the magazine.

The traverse mechanism (Fig. 1-1) drives the optical pickup base by the rack gear which is driven by the
motor via the worm gear, gear A, and gear B. The gear A and gear B are double clutch gears.
The inner REST switch is turned on by the optical pickup base when the optical nickup is driven inner-

The largest difference in optical structure between the 3-beam type and single beam type is that
single beam type has no diffraction grating. Therefore, the single beam type has only one beam on
optical path, and its photo-detector is divided into four instead of six {four plus two).
The two sub-beams of the 3-beam type have the function of generating tracking errors signal. The
process of generating tracking error signal by the single beam type that is without sub-beams is
described in Section 1-4. Focus error signal generated by the conventional astigma method.
3-Beam type has a small RF detector area (150 um squared). Therefore, it has a disadvantage when
playing discs with fingerprints.
1-Beam type (4-segments) overcomes the fingerprint playability but it has a disadvantage when
playing scratched discs. The area of the 4-segment photodetector is large (1000 um squared).
Therefore, the error generated by fingerprints is included and corrected. Since the focus and track-
ing detectors are included as part of the RF detector, the spike is detected as an error signal.
1-Beam type (6-segments) has a reduced size RF detector (250 um squared) and two large and
separate detectors have been added. Any spikes generated by a scratched disc do not appear as a

text:
1-3. Photo Detector
The photo Detector is probably the single most important component in the campact disc player. The
reason for this is that all intelligence needed to operate the unit is developed from the returning laser beam
by the photo detector. This will include focus error signal, tracking error signal as well as the intelligence
signal. °
The single beam type (Fig. 1-3b) has a large PD surface area to prevent RF signal level reduction. However,
if the beam irradiated at a scratch or other defects on the disc surface, the servo errors occur and decrease
playability.
In order to compensate such divergent conditions, the photo-detector structure shown in Figure 1-3c is
used, the four parts in the center are used for error detection, and the total sum including the periphery
(B1 + B2) is the RF signal.

4. CIRCUIT OPERATIONS (TYPE A)
4-1 Traverse Control Circuit (Fig. 4-1)
To the optical pickup at the starting position, RF must be present to operate the traverse motor. The IN
SW changes (H) > (L) > (H) by the movement of optical pickup block.
When SW4 becomes (L), and IN SW is (H). TRV R (L) and TRV F (H) are output from 1C601, the
traverse motor drives the optical pick from outside to inside.
When IN SW turns (L), TRV R turns (H) and TRV F turns (L), and the optical pick moves from inside to
outside. When IN SW is (H) again, the optical pick up is at the starting position, the traverse motor has
ended the starting position setting operation, i.e. both TRV R and TRV F have become (L).
During the setting operation CNT 1, 2, 3, and 4 are all at (H); but just as soon as completion of the opera-
tion, CNT 1 remains at (H), while CNT 2, 3, and 4 change to (L).

Meantime, the laser emission instruction LD ON at pin 28 of 1C601 joins the LD APC circuit at pin 31 of
1C1 LD ON. The laser power supplies at pin 7 of |C1, the laser emits.
The focus control circuit detects this state with the photo-detector and joins the FE signal at pin 15 of
iC1 into 1C601. And it detects the “S-curve” when the proper disk exists, and search oscillation as well as
laser emission are normal. The detecting operation ends when (L) > (H) pulse from the SENSE applied
to the micro-computer.

A4-4 Description of New Servo Circuit
(MN8373S and MN8374S)
1. General
The servo circuit in CQ-E850, CQ-DP25/26
has been entirely
changed with new IC's for
performance improvement and
compactness.
2. Circuit Configuration
The servo circuit used in the
conventional FF-1 CD players comprised a
servo IC (AN8370S) and discrete circuit.
In contrast, the modified servo circuit
consists of three IC chips with on
discrete circuit.
(1). IC-1 (servo amplifier)
=Processes analog servo signals.
(2). IC-601 (servo controller)
=Processes digital servo signals.
(3). IC-602 (servo driver)
=Drives the focus, tracking, and
traverse coils.
The block diagram of IC-1 (AN8373S) and
IC-601 (AN8374S) are shows figure 4-9.
3. Departures from the Conventional Servo
Circuit and some Cautions
While the new servo circuit replaces
discrete components integrated circuits,
the basic circuit configurations and
operations are almost identical to those
of the conventional servo circuit, with
the exception of the following details:
PLL adjustment eliminated

pulled into the PLL lock range by
using the CLK (88.2KHz) signal.

9. Tracking Servo Circuit Operation
The focus balance circuit output,
Al + A2 and A3 + A4, are also
transferred to the tracking
balance circuit. The output of
the tracking balance circuit are
applied to the phase difference
limiter within IC-601, where they
are phase compared to produce a
tracking error signal.
The tracking error signal at
IC-601 pin 4 is subjected to gain
adjustment, then applied to the
loop filter, within IC-101 via
the tracking switch.
The loop filter output appearing
at IC-601 pin 22, is coupled to
pin 42 (BR IN/ tracking error
input) of IC-601, where it is fed
into a braking circuit. The
output of the braking circuit
appears at pin 41 (BR oUuT/
tracking drive control signal)
and couples to the tracking coil
driver to drive the tracking
actuator's.
10. Traverse Servo Circuit Operation
PLAY mode:
The tracking error signal applied
to IC-601 pin 42 goes through the
traverse switch and TRV (traverse
circuit) filter (for response
compensation) and appears at pin
39. This output is used to
control the traverse actuator.
KICK mode:
The KICK signal decoded from the
system CPU command by the control
logic appears at pin 27. It is
used to control the tracking
actuator which KICKs the pick-up
by a span of 1, 10, or 100 tracks
according to the system CPU
command.
Forced traverse mode:
The TRVF, TRVR signals supplied
from system CPU to pins 34 and

Forced traverse mode:
The TRVF, TRVR signals supplied
from system CPU to pins 34 and
35, respectively, are decoded to
produce a traverse drive signal.
The signal appears at pin 25 and
drives the traverse coil.

11. RF Signal Detection and Auto Focus
Circuit
The auto focus circuit within IC-601
performs focus search. If it detects an
FE signal S-Curve it closes the focus
switch contacts to close the focus servo
loop. At this point the RF detector
within IC-101 detects the RF signal and
supplies it to the F.LOCK DET. input at
IC-601 pin 36.
The F.LOCK signal is used to indicate to
system CPU that focus is "IN". If focus
goes "OUT" and the RF signal is no longer
detected, the auto focus circuit opens
the focus loop switch and starts focus
search again.
12. Dropout Detection Circuit
(1). Black Band Dropout (BDO)
Dropouts are detected from the RF
Signal within Ic-101. In order to
stabilize the tracking servo against
dropout; the BDO signal is supplied
from IC-601 pin 37 to the phase
difference limitter and used to hold
the tracking servo operation.
- Signal Dropout (SDO)
If an RF signal dropout is detected
by the RF detector, or a BDO is
detected, the SDO signal is supplied
to the signal processor to stabilize
the CLV servo operation.

A4-5 Digital Filtering and D/A Converter
| 1) Principle of the Digital Filter
The way an audio wave is converted to a
digital signal, processed digitally, and
then returned toa high-purity audio
form, is more and more widely
understood.
The conversion from analogue into
digital signals is often called pulse
code modulation, or PCM. The analogue
waveform is first sampled (measured at
regular intervals). Then it is
quantized. This means that it is given
the nearest numerical value in the large
range of numbers used to transmit the
digital sound information. The quantized
value is then converted to binary form
and encoded into a pulse train
representing the series of numbers. This
process of analogue’ to digital
conversion is shows in figure 5-1.

analogue conversion.
2) How the Number of Bits Affects S/N
The accuracy of a digital system depends
on the number of bits used for the
binary number. This is because the
number of bits determines the accuracy
with which the samples taken from the
Original waveform can be quantized, i.e.
expressed in digital form.
Two bits give four 2 possible values for
use in quantization, also three bits
give eight 2 possible values.
Every bit added doubles the number of
possible values. In audio terms, this
adds 6dB to the signal to noise ratio,
because it reduces the quantization
noise by a factor of 2.
The sixteen bits as used in the CD
system give 65536 (216 ) possible values
for quantization, anda signal to noise
ratio of 96dB. The audio signals are
encoded in the actual CD with this
ratio.
960B is approximation. An additional
factor, which depends on the type of
Signal, is always present, regardless of
the number of bits; for sine wave
signals this makes the -theoretical

text:
3) The Effect of the Sampling
Frequency
Another important factor is sampling
frequency, for efficiency in digital
operations, this is kept low (44,1KHz)
at a little over twice the maximum audio
frequency (20.0KHZ). During the sampling
process this frequency and its harmonics
or multiples become modulated with the
original waveform in a series of
frequency bands as shows figure 19-2.
The bottom end of the lowest band is
rather close to the top of the audio
frequency range.
Figure 5-2
Figure 5-2 shows the frequency spectrum
produced by sampling showing the
periodic repetitions of the audio band.
The bottom end of the lowest band is
close to the audio frequency range.
In a digital audio system the audible
noise has a different character to the
familiar noise in an analogue audio
system. The digital audio system
background noise is called quantization
noise.
The quantization noise of a system can
be defined as the error signal between
the original waveform before the
analogue to digital conversion process,
and the restored waveform after the
digital to analogue conversion process.
This error signal can be considered as
both noise and distortion at the same
time.
Figure 5-3
Figure 5-3 shows the quantization
noise, The difference between the
original audio waveform and the
regenerated wave after D/A conversion
(a) causes quantization noise (b).
The 16 bits analogue to digital

regenerated wave after D/A conversion
(a) causes quantization noise (b).
The 16 bits analogue to digital
conversion at the recording stage
delivers a 16 bits digital signal with
an intrinsic accuracy or signal to noise
ration of maximum 96dB.
An ideal digital to analogue converter
(D/A) would deliver an analogue output
signal without adding noise to it.
However, ideal D/A do not exist a small
but finite electronic inaccuracy adds
noise to the quantization noise of the
digital signal.
The inaccuracy of a 16 bits D/A (the
resolution limit of half the least
Significant bit) can be interpreted as a
noise source that reduces the signal to
noise ratio of the D/A to 96dB.

and a sampling frequency of 44.1KHz, the

repetitions of the audio frequencies

These frequency bands can overload the

audible interference. They must be
filtered out.

When a laser ON mode command (H, L, L, L) is received, pin 5 goes high to turn the laser on.
A loop circuit is formed by Q and D (the laser paired with a PIN diode) and the APC in the IC, and laser

C4-1-3. RF Amplifier and Dropout Detector Circuits
(1) RF amplifier circuit
RF signal is the total sum of all the 6-segment photo-detector (A1 + A2 + A3 + A4 + B1 + B2) of
the optical pickup. The resulting RF signal is applied to pin 33, via Q, (OQ is located in the optical
pickup.) where it is amplified by an RF amplifier having gain of approx 34 dB.
The output of the RF amplifier appears at pin 31, and couples to pin 15 of |1C AN8371S.
(2) Dropout detector circuit
The dropout detector detects signal dropouts in the RF signal, stabilizes the tracking servo against
dropouts, and provides the defection signal to pin 32.
The detection dropout process is shown in Fig. 6-5. The level goes high if a dropout is detected.

Tracking error circuit
Tracking error circuit inputs the I-V converted signals to pin 2 and 4 viaC119 and C117. The com-
parators shape the waveforms.
In the tracking error process of the single beam type, the phase difference between the two signals
is detected and a pulse corresponding to the phase difference is generated as described in section. 1-4,
Deviating direction is judged from the polarity of the pulse. The generated pulse is smoothed by the
LPF into an analog tracking error (TE) signal. This is how the phase comparator and LPF operate.
Then, the TE signal is output from pin 6 (TE OUT) via the TE amplifier and TE SW.
VR102 is the tracking gain (TR GAIN) control, and VR106 the tracking offset (TR OFFSET)
control.
Kick and hold circuits
Kick means jumping the beam from one track to another during a pause or manual search. The kick
timing is set by a control signal from the microcomputer, and a kick signal is appeared pin 20. The
waveform of each kick signal is shown in Fig. 4-10.
The hold circuit holds the preceding TE signal during kick made. TE SW is turned off during kick
mode. Signal wave forms in pause kick are shown in Fig. 4-11.

Brake circuit
The brake circuit brakes the tracking actuator to quickly retract the tracking servo after rapid feed
or kick (10/100). The process is shown in Fig. 4-12.
The brake circuit applies a single limiter (indicated by the dotted line in the figure) to the TE signal
to absorb the energy after kick.
The figure shows the brake in the KICK REV mode. In the KICK FWD mode, the brake is applied
with the single limiter inverted in polarity. Therefore, the brake circuit requires a kick direction
discriminating signal, which is generated from a tracking cross signal and off track signal as shown in
Fig. 4-13.
The cross signal phase leads in the KICK FWD mode and lags in the KICK REV mode. The brake
direction is determined by detecting the above phase difference.

C4-2-2. Mode Select Circuit
The multiplexer (I[C603) is used for mode selection.

The output from pin 1, 1C601 is applied to the drive circuit when pin 10 and pin 9 of IC603 are

A brief description of CD recording system signal processing is given in the following.
1) The CD sampling frequency is 44.1 kHz, and quantizing involves A—D conversion to 16 bits

The 16 bits are divided into upper 8 bits and lower 8 bits.

12 samples of data (six each for the right and left) are taken as a frame for signal processing. In
other words, 24-symbol data constitutes a frame. W1 to W24 shown in Fig. 4-3 correspond to
it.
Data W1 to W24 are first scrambled by C2. Scramble may be considered to be a small interjeave.
In C2 scramble, the data are delayed over two frames alternately in terms of sample data.
After C2 scramble, the data enter the C2 encoder, which generates 4-symbol parity signals
Q1 to Q4 from the 24-symbol data using reed solomon code, and arranges them in the frame
center.
The symbol data count in one frame is 28 in total.
Next is the interleave.
As shown in the figure, the interleave delays the 28-symbol data, including the Q parity signals,
over the range of 4 frames minimum to 108 frames maximum.
The C1 encoder generates 4-symbol parity signals P1 to P4 from the 28-symbol data, which
have been rearranged by interleaving, using reed solomon code, and arranges them at the frame
end.
Here, the symbol data count in a frame is 32 in total. (See Fig. 4-3.)

Fig. 4-4 EFM Modulation
EFM is a new modulation system for CD, and stands for Eight to Fourteenth Modulation meaning
modulating 8 symbol data bits to 14 channel bits.
EFM is necessary because the data bit arrangement of 1's and O’s cannot be defined if symbol data
remains as such.
If 1’s or O's continue so long, data will be a direct current so that self-clocks cannot be generated by
the tracking servo (using pits) and reproducing system.
Conversely, if 1’s and O's are frequently reversed, it will be necessary to reduce the laser beam to a
very small diameter.

text:
The CLV servo is a rotation speed control servo for maintaining linear speed of the disk constant.
The servo is divided into three parts, that is 11T servo, CLV servo, and traverse tracking servo. The
traverse tracking servo and 11T servo are rough servos, and the CLV servo is a fine servo. The CLV
control which is the primary part of the circuit in the LSI. The CLV servo circuits consists of micro-
computers AN8371S and AN8281S.
Figure 9-17 shows the CLV servo circuit.
1) AN8281S circuit operation

AN82815S is the spindle motor drive IC. The control voltage EC is applied from the CLV control
circuit is applied to pin 8, and the reference voltage divided by R506 and R507 (DCR) is applied
to pin 4.
FG and rotating direction are detected by the Hall element, and the FG signal is fed back to the
CLV control circuit from pin 13.
The ON/OFF function of this IC (pin 15) controls start and stop of the motor.
Fig. 4-18 shows EC signal versus the motor.

11T servo
The 11t servo changes the constant speed to constant linear speed.
This requires some signal extracted from the disk, that is, SRF signal. (SRF signal is generated
by data-slicing RF signal.)
The 11T servo controls the SRF signals that the longest period of the signal will be equivalent 11
times the period of the reference clock 1T (4.3 MHz).

The 11T servo controls the SRF signals that the longest period of the signal will be equivalent 11
times the period of the reference clock 1T (4.3 MHz).
When the 11T servo operates, the spindle motor comes close to the control speed of the fine
servo.
CLV servo
The CLV servo is started by the 11T servo when digital signals are ready for processing in the
LSI.
For digital signal processing, data is once written in an external RAM and read out again. A
RAM address generator circuit is provided in the LSI for this purpose. Because a crystal clock
is used for reading data and a clock synchronized with reproducing signals (corresponding to
PCK) is used for writing data, the address locations fluctuates in RAM. The fine servo detects
the address location signals and operates to keep the read/wirte pace constant.
Traverse tracking servo
The traverse tracking servo follows the pick-up and controls the tinear speed of the pick-up
constant when the traverse mechanism at high speed,
This servo operates in such a way that two continuous minimum periods of the SRF will be 6
times the period of the reference clock 1T (4.3 MHz).
TRON is used for switching the traverse tracking servo to the 11T servo or vice versa. That is,
the traverse tracking servo is selected when TRON is high and the 11T servo is selected when
TRON is low.

C4-5-3 LPF and De-emphasis Circuit
The lowpass filter(LPF) restores the signals containing harmonics (step waves) received from the deglitch
circuit to a complete audio signal.
The LPF also has a de-emphasis function. It reads emphasis or no emphasis from subcode (O channel)
recorded on the disk, and the control signal is output from pin 21 (DEMPHA) of IC601 (LSI). De-
mphasis is applied when the control signal is high.
