A6 TROUBLESHOOTING (TYPE A)
A6-1 SYMPTOM CHECK
When traverse motor malfunctions. Check IN SW (H).
Also, when the IN SW is not in changing stage, check the system CPU Pins 18 and 19 (TRV R, TRV
F), and Pins 14-17 (CNT1, 2, 3, 4, all H) outputs to 1C601, then from 1C601 (TRV F/R) to IC602,
from |C602 to the traverse motor.
When the focus lens moves up and down repeatedly, check if the disk is properly set. If the LD ON
terminal of Pin 28 IC601 is (H), check the LD terminal of Pin 7 IC1. To see if APC circuit is turned
on to intensify the laser.
Check connections between the photo-detector and IC1, check if there is a pulse at the FE terminal
of Pin 15 1C1, and a pulse at SENSE terminal of Pin 24 1C601.
If the disk ejects, when CNT1 is (H), CNT2, 3, and 4 are (L). Check to see if the CLW terminal of Pin
10 1C601, the FPO terminal of Pin 24 1C1, and FD terminal of Pin 10 1C602 generate the triangular
wave respectively.
If the disk ejects at the time when the disk detection ended (CNT1, 2, 3, and 4 (H)), check connec-
tion between IC2 and spindle motor, |C2 and 1C501 Pin 32 L/R (Clock pulse), Pin 65 EC (Start-up
control pulse) and Pin 64 PC (L)).
Also trace and check Pin 23 MLD, Pin 24 MCLK and Pin 25 MDATA (data pulse) of the micro-
computer.
If the disk ejects at the time when CNT1 is (L), CNT2, 3, and 4 are (H), check to see if 1C601 Pin 26

1. When making any connections, be sure to turn off all power source.

However, when the car is driving on a very rough road conditions will sometimes cause the player to
skip the music. However, the disc and the CD Player will not be damaged by these conditions.
(Example: Pothole, railroad crossing, road paved with stone, etc.)

title: Troubleshooting Guide CD Players 1986-1990 (MSC910101)
section: Intro Introduction, models (all CD players 1986-1990), possible symptoms (skipping, TOC read but
text:
Introduction
The widespread popularity of Hi-Fi Digital Audio has made the compact disc player a
common place component in today’s audio systems. Fortunately, in the years since its
initial introduction, the serviceability of the compact disc player has improved
dramatically, mostly due to advances in digital technology. What this technology was not
capable of doing however, is to do away with the various mechanical and electrical
adjustments required on these units.
This guide is meant to eliminate trial-and-error servicing procedures and aid in the
repairing of compact disc players by standardizing the procedure. If followed correctly,
the optimum operating condition of the unit can be achieved by using this guide. For this
reason, it is important that all of the procedures listed in this guide be performed
BEFORE replacing any optical pickup assemblies.
Included along with this procedure is a useful reference chart containing pickup part
numbers and related information.
NOTE: THE FOLLOWING PROCEDURES CONTAIN GENERAL INFORMATION.
FOR SPECIFIC DETAILS PLEASE REFER TO THE CORRESPONDING
SERVICE MANUAL FOR YOUR UNIT.
Models
All compact disc players from 1986 to 1990.
Possible Symptoms
1. Skipping.
2. TOC is read, but disc does not play.
3. No TOC.
4. Poor playability.

the guide rails by applying the prescribed traverse oil (see page 8).

A. Test focus and tracking servo circuits
Playing the 0.9mm wedge (track 8) on the playability test disc serves to show
how well the unit is at tracking defects on discs. If skipping occurs, first
inspect the test disc for scratches or dust. If skipping persists, it may be
necessary to perform the mechanical adjustment over again (See Step 3C).
B. Perform PLL adjustment
Play the 0.8mm wedge on the playability test disc and connect the
oscilloscope to the PLL test point. Adjust the PLL variable resistor so its
position is between the two locations where the PLL waveform starts to be
disturbed. This adjustment is used to set the operating range of the voltage
controlled oscillator that allows the disc to be synchronized with the

I. MECHANICAL ADJUSTMENTS
™ When the optical pick-up and peripheral mechanism parts incorporated in the traverse deck are replaced
or removed, such as the spindle motor, it is necessary to confirm the adjustment related to the optical
pick-up and then readjust as required.
1. Turntable Height Adjustment
A. Purpose
The outjut from the laser diode is focused on the signal side of the disc, via the focus lens. Focussing is
accomplished by moving the focus lens vertically. The focus servo is used to control such vertical movement.
Since the focus servo is designed to operate within a limited range, it is necessary to adjust the lens at the
mechanical midpoint position of the servo’s respective operating range. If this adjustment should be
deviated, skipping may occur during play or in an extreme case, no turntable rotation.

A. Purpose
Regardless of disc warpage (+/— 0.4mm) due to manufacturing tolerances, the focus servo must
operate to constantly keep the lens focused on the disc’s pits. The greater the servo’s gain, the
easier the lens can focus on the disc; however it becomes unstable due to unwanted signals. The
gain is therefore set to unity (0 dB=1, @750Hz) at which point stability is acceptable and the gain
is adequate.

The reason why the focus servo must be adjusted using a 750 Hz tone is because this is the frequency

A. Purpose
During disc manufacturing, disc eccentricity results due to tooling tolerances. Eccentricity also results if
the disc does not rest exactly in the center of the CD player’s spindle.
The tracking servo is designed to overcome these tolerances and keep the lens on track.
B. Principle of the Tracking gain adjustment
The tracking servo loop is opened at which point a 1KHz, 1.2KHz or 1.5KHz signal is fed. This point is
TP2 of the “servo gain adjuster’.
The signal, once through the servo, appears at TP1. The tracking gain control is to be adjusted so that the
level of TP1 equals that of TP2, at which point the gain is one (OdB)

4. Focus offset adjustment
A. Purpose
The CD player must be able to compensate for manufacturing imperfections of disc and dust or any other
contaminants on the signal side.
As the pick-up traces the track, if dust or disc imperfections are present, the focusing depth changes.
Without proper focus the tracking servo is affected as well;causing the pick-up to move to a different track.
When the lens detects imperfections as mentions above, the focus servo is enabled in order to maintain
proper focusing within the operating range of the servo.
The focus offset alignment is therefore necessary to adjust the servo’s operating reference point.

A. Purpose
During playback operation, the laser beam must follow the track exactly at its center.
If it is not, proper tracking can not be accomplished, and skipping may occur during playback of the
disc which has manufacturing imperfections and dust or any other contaminants on the signal side.
B. Basic principle of adjustment
A 1 KHz signal is applied to the tracking servo circuit to intentionally cause the beam to oscillate from
side to side of the track being traced (see fig. 2-6-1). This is done to simulate an error signal so that the
tracking servo can be adjusted for minimum gain (minimum swing) at 1 KHz.
